opus-5.5.text:
I think the logic of pricing has really shifted. In the pretraining era, people mostly thought about cost per token in terms of model size: how many parameters, how much compute per forward pass. A smaller model is cheaper, so you charge less. That was more or less the whole story.

Once you move into the post-training era, especially with reasoning and agentic use, that framing isn't enough. What users actually pay for isn't a single token. It's a completed task. A model that's cheap per token but has to think for a very long time, or needs many retries to finish a coding task or an agent workflow, isn't actually cheap. So for something like Flash, the question we ask is: what does it cost to get a job done well?

That changes where you put effort. On the architecture side, you care a lot about inference efficiency: how attention scales with long context, how fast decoding is, how well it fits the hardware. Long contexts and long reasoning chains are now the normal case, not the edge case. On the post-training side, you care about the model being efficient with its thinking. Don't overthink easy problems, don't waste tokens, and be reliable enough that you don't need several attempts.

So the basis for pricing is really the whole system: model design, training, and serving together. If you do that well, you can offer a price that looks aggressive, but it's not a subsidy. It reflects real efficiency. I also think low cost matters strategically. When intelligence gets cheap enough, people start using it in ways they wouldn't before, like running many agents in parallel or letting a model iterate for a long time. That usage then tells you what to improve in the next round of training. Price isn't just a business number. It shapes what the model gets used for, and that feeds back into how the model evolves.

r002.rationale: It discusses long-context inference efficiency, but does not identify the quality of the context as a post-training pricing consideration.

r003.rationale: It discusses efficient reasoning and task reliability, but does not say that how well a model understands its context affects post-training pricing.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the pricing logic for Flash has changed quite a bit as the center of gravity shifted from pretraining to post-training.

In the pretraining era, pricing was almost a direct function of scale. You trained a bigger model, inference cost more per token, and you set a price that covered compute plus some margin. Flash as a category existed to be the cheap option — small, fast, "good enough" for high-volume tasks. The price was basically a signal of how small the model was.

With post-training taking over, that relationship breaks down. A lot of the capability now comes from RL, distillation, and data quality rather than parameter count. So a Flash-sized model can be surprisingly strong on the tasks people actually pay for — agentic workflows, tool calling, long-context extraction — while its inference cost stays low. That means the cost basis and the value basis diverge. Cost is still anchored to the model's size and serving efficiency, but the value is anchored to what the post-trained model can reliably do.

So how do we think about price? Three things. First, we still price off cost, because for Flash the whole point is that volume users can run it everywhere without thinking about it. If we priced on capability, we'd kill the use cases that make it Flash. Second, we look at where the model sits in the agent loop. A lot of Flash tokens are not final answers — they're intermediate steps, retries, verification passes. If each of those is cheap, people build more elaborate systems, and total consumption goes up. That's the business we want. Third, post-training costs are amortized differently. RL on a small model is actually quite expensive relative to its size, but it's a one-time investment spread over enormous token volume, so it barely moves the per-token price.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that "smarter must mean more expensive." Post-training has made that less true. The right framing is that Flash pricing should reflect the marginal cost of serving, and the capability gain from post-training should show up as more usage, not a higher unit price. If you get that wrong and raise prices because the model got better, you just push developers to distill their own.

r002.rationale: It mentions data quality and long-context tasks, but does not identify context quality as a pricing consideration.

r003.rationale: It discusses long-context extraction, but does not identify how well the model understands its context as a pricing consideration.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is what the price reflects. In pretraining, you can think about it largely in terms of scale: how much compute goes into training the model, and how much it costs to serve. With post-training, that relationship becomes less straightforward, because you can improve what a model can actually do without increasing its size proportionally.

So for Flash, I’d separate the cost of providing the model from the value it delivers. Inference efficiency gives you room to offer a low price. Post-training can make that inexpensive model useful for a much wider range of tasks. And from the user’s perspective, the meaningful measure is increasingly the cost of completing a task successfully, rather than just the price per token. A cheap response that needs several retries may end up being more expensive than a slightly pricier response that works the first time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is what you’re pricing: the cost of producing tokens, or the value of the capability behind those tokens. Pretraining gives a model a broad foundation, but post-training can make that foundation much more useful for a particular task. So parameter count alone becomes a less useful basis for comparing prices.

For Flash, I would look at the cost of getting a task done successfully. A lower token price is valuable, but you also have to consider how many tokens the model needs, how often it retries, and whether the result is good enough. Post-training can change all of those things. The pricing has to balance efficient inference with the capability users actually experience.
